མི་འཐད་དོ། །འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། སྡུག་བསྔལ་དེ་ལས་གང་ཟག་དེ་གཞན་གྱི་#མ་ཡིན་པས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བྱས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྣམ་གྲངས་ལས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བདག་གིས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་ཀྱང་སྨྲ་ཞིང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་གང་ཟག་མ་ཡིན་པས་རྣམ་གྲངས་ལས་
སྡུག་བསྔལ་གཞན་གྱིས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་ཀྱང་སྨྲའོ། །འདིར་བཤད་པ། རེ་ཞིག་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བདག་བྱས་མིན། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་#ནི་དེ་མ་བྱས། །རེ་ཞིག་སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྣམ་གྲངས་ལས་བདག་གིས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་མི་འཐད་དེ། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་དེ་མ་བྱས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྣམ་གྲངས་ལས་གཞན་གྱིས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་གང་སྨྲས་པ་དེ་ལ་ཡང་དཔྱད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། གལ་ཏེ་གཞན་བདག་མ་བྱས་ན། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་གཞན་བྱས་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །གཞན་གྱིས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་དེ་ཡང་གལ་ཏེ་གཞན་ཏེ། བདག་ཉིད་མ་བྱས་
ཤིང་མ་གྲུབ་ན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དེ་གཞན་གྱིས་བྱས་པར་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། སྡུག་བསྔལ་བདག་དང་གཞན་གཉི་ག་འདུས་པས་བྱས་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །འདིར་བཤད་པ། གལ་ཏེ་རེ་རེས་བྱས་གྱུར་ན། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་གཉི་གས་བྱས་པར་འགྱུར། །གལ་ཏེ་རེ་རེས་བྱས་པ་
ཡོད་པར་འགྱུར་#ན་ནི། སྡུག་བསྔལ་གཉི་གས་བྱས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཞིག་ན། གང་གི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ལ་#མ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བདག་དང་གཞན་གཉི་གས་#འདུས་པས་བྱས་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། དེ་ལྟར་བདག་དང་གཞན་དང་གཉི་གས་བྱས་པར་མི་རིགས་ན། འོ་ན་
སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ལས་བྱུང་#བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིར་བཤད་པ། གཞན་གྱིས་མ་བྱས་བདག་མ་བྱས། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྒྱུ་མེད་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །དེ་ལྟར་གཞན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་མ་བྱས་བདག་གིས་ཀྱང་མ་བྱས་ན། སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བར་ག་ལ་འཐད་དེ། སྐྱོན་ཆེན་
པོར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་འབའ་ཞིག་རྣམ་པ་བཞི། །ཡོད་མ་ཡིན་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། །ཕྱི་རོལ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་། །རྣམ་པ་བཞི་པོ་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཕུང་པོ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་འབའ་ཞིག་ལ། །བདག་དང་གཞན་དང་གཉི་ག་དང་རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་

It is illogical. To this, it is said: "Since that person is not something other than suffering, and since suffering is created by suffering, it is said in one sense that suffering is self-created. Since that which is suffering is not the person, it is also said in another sense that suffering is created by another." To this, it is explained:

Suffering is not self-created,
For it was not created by that very thing.

First, the claim that suffering is self-created in one sense is illogical. Why? Because it was not created by that very same thing <note>the self cannot act upon itself as both subject and object</note>. One must also examine the claim that suffering is created by another in a different sense:

If the other were not self-created,
How could suffering be created by another?

If that which is fixated upon as "another" were not itself created and established, how could that suffering be created by another? To this, it is said: "Suffering exists as something created by the combination of both self and other." To this, it is explained:

If it were created by each one,
Then suffering would be created by both.

If it were the case that it was created by each one <note>individually</note>, then it would follow that suffering is created by both. Since that is not the case, suffering created by the combination of both self and other also does not exist. To this, it is said: "If it is unreasonable for it to be created by self, other, or both, then suffering must arise without a cause." To this, it is explained:

If it is not created by another or by self,
How could suffering be causeless?

If it is not created by another and not created by self, how could it be reasonable for suffering to arise without a cause? This would result in a great logical fallacy.

Not only are the four modes
Non-existent for suffering,
But for external things as well,
Those four modes do not exist.

For the aggregates of suffering alone, those four modes—arising from self, other, both, or without cause—
tail: are not only non-existent, but for external things such as form and so on, those four modes also do not exist.
old_translation:
It is incorrect. Here someone says: Since the person is not something other than that suffering, and because suffering is created by suffering, it is said in one sense that suffering is self-created. However, since the person is not identical to the suffering itself, it is also said in another sense that suffering is created by another <note>this refers to the classical debate in Madhyamaka philosophy regarding the origins of suffering</note>.

To this we respond:
First, suffering is not self-created.
The self does not create itself.
The assertion that suffering is self-created in a certain sense is incorrect. Why is that? Because it is not created by itself <note>in Buddhist logic, a thing cannot act upon itself; a knife cannot cut its own edge</note>.

We must also examine the claim that suffering is created by another in a certain sense.
If the "other" is not self-established,
How could suffering be created by another?
If one is attached to the idea that it is created by another, yet that "other" itself is not self-made or established, how could that suffering be something created by an "other"?

Here someone says: Suffering exists as something created by the combination of both self and other.

To this we respond:
If it were created by each one individually,
Then suffering would be created by both together.
If it were possible for suffering to be created by each one <note>self and other</note> independently, then it could be created by both together. Since that is not the case, suffering is not created by the combination of both self and other.

Here someone says: Since it is unreasonable for it to be created by self, other, or both, then suffering must arise without a cause.

To this we respond:
If not created by another and not created by self,
How could suffering be without a cause?
Since it is not created by another and not created by self, how could it be reasonable for suffering to arise without a cause? This would lead to the fallacy of great errors <note>such as the denial of karma and the law of cause and effect</note>.

Not only for suffering are these four aspects
Non-existent;
Even for external entities,
These four aspects do not exist.
Whether for the aggregates of suffering alone,
Or for external things, creation through self, other, both, or causelessness does not exist.

<summary>This page presents a philosophical refutation of the four possible origins of suffering: self-creation, creation by another, creation by both, or causeless arising. It argues that none of these positions are logically tenable, extending this critique to all external phenomena.</summary>
<keywords>Madhyamaka, suffering, causation, self-creation, fourfold negation, aggregates, logic</keywords>
